episodes.210091: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of March 11, 2026. Damaging winds was the primary threat with this line, particularly across southern Middle Tennessee. Several reports of downed trees, downed powerlines, and roof damage were received. Small hail also occurred with this line of storms with several reports of dime to nickel size hail received in the Hendersonville area.
episodes.210118: On the morning of March 11, 2026, an unseasonably warm and moist airmass with strong deep-layer shear produced a severe weather outbreak. A quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) pushed across central Indiana producing widespread damaging wind gusts with significant tree damage and some structural damage. There were also a few reports of flooded roads across portions of south-central Indiana.
episodes.210132: During the afternoon hours of March 10th, supercells brought massive hail to portions of eastern Kansas.
episodes.210266: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
episodes.210267: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
episodes.210268: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in gale- to storm-force winds over the upper Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.210341: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.
episodes.210342: A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
episodes.210343: Scattered severe thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the evening of March 10th.
episodes.210472: A series of cold fronts would move across Arkansas over this period of severe weather which brought large hail, damaging wind gusts, flash flooding, and even produced a tornado near Fordyce. This bout of severe weather was spread across the entire state of Arkansas over this period.
episodes.210530: A line of thunderstorms moved along the US Highway 54 corridor during the late evening of March 10th. Damaging winds occurred along this line of storms with damage to trees and structures.
episodes.210606: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
episodes.210740: During the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, an occluded surface low drifted eastward from near Green Bay to northwestern Lower MI. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward from northwest PA into southwestern NY, while the low's cold front swept eastward from northeastern IN to north-central OH. Ahead of the cold front and within the warm sector, a line of multicell rain showers and thunderstorms generated sporadic straight-line convective wind damage in Wyandot and Marion Counties to Ashland County as the line persisted generally eastward in northern OH. Behind the line, a cluster of multicell rain showers generated a severe-caliber peak straight-line convective wind gust at the Lorain County Airport ASOS as the cluster of showers persisted generally northeastward. These showers and storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate effective bulk shear and weak MUCAPE.
episodes.210745: During the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, an occluded surface low drifted eastward from near Green Bay to northwestern Lower MI. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward from northwest PA into southwestern NY, while the low's cold front swept eastward from northeastern IN to north-central OH. Along the warm front and within the warm sector, scattered multicell rain showers and thunderstorms persisted generally northeastward across NW PA during the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak MUCAPE. A severe-caliber peak straight-line convective wind gust occurred at the Meadville Airport ASOS.
episodes.210757: An isolated storm developed on the evening of March 10 in far eastern Douglas County. This produced small hail in Douglas County before producing much larger hail farther east outside of the TOP forecast area. A few hours later, more widespread storms developed along a cold front in eastern KS. These produced more small hail, as well as an isolated corridor of very strong 65-85 mph winds that caused notable damage in Anderson County.
episodes.210768: Showers and storms developed ahead of a cold front during the morning of March 11th, with subsequent rounds of scattered activity progressing across the area throughout the day. A few strong to severe storms downed trees in Perry and Morgan Counties during the early afternoon. More storms and moderate to heavy showers then overspread the area as an upper level disturbance steered the front through overnight. Between a half inch and one and a quarter inches of rain fell across southeast Ohio, with heavier precipitation prompting minor flooding of Duck Creek in Washington County and Sunday Creek in Athens County. Impacts primarily included flooding of a few roads, fields, and low-lying areas next to the creeks. Precipitation tapered off from west to east behind the front, coming to an end in southeast Ohio early in the morning of the 12th.
episodes.210778: A low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region, prompting showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced damaging winds and heavy rainfall, leading to instances of flooding.
episodes.210791: Surface low pressure stationed in southern Ontario with a cold front stationed across the Great Lakes and a warm front analyzed across the northern half of New York State allowed for all of central Pennsylvania to have maximum residence timing in the warm sector. Ample low-level and bulk shear in place across the region and lift allowed for numerous showers and thunderstorms to begin forming during the afternoon hours of March 11, 2026. Cloud cover across much of central Pennsylvania did tamper instability to where thunderstorms were slow to push towards severe limits; however, with daytime heating in between breaks in the clouds, instability pushed closer to the 700-1000 J/kg range and allowed for severe thunderstorms south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Multiple instances of tree damage within severe thunderstorms were reported in portions of Cambria, Somerset, Bedford, and Blair counties before a slight decrease in intensity occurred in south-central Pennsylvania where cloud cover remained more persistent. Thunderstorms began to intensify in portions of the Lower Susquehanna Valley, where multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Dauphin and Lebanon counties during the evening hours.
episodes.210815: An upper-level low-pressure center progressed eastward through the Plains on the afternoon and evening of March 10, leading to the development of thunderstorms. These storms were able to initiate along a dryline across the Big Country. As the storms moved east through the forecast area, some generated large hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.210933: On the evening of March 10th, a discrete supercell moved from Illinois into northwest Indiana. It produced an EF-2 tornado in Starke County with maximum winds of 115 mph, prompting a rare Tornado Emergency for the area near Knox, IN. Following the initial supercell, a line of storms moved through on the morning of March 11th. Training storms produced significant rainfall between 1 and 3, with localized amounts reaching 4-5, resulting in Flash Flood Warnings and Flood Advisories.
episodes.210946: During the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, an occluded surface low drifted eastward from near Green Bay to northwestern Lower MI. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward from northwest PA into southwestern NY, while the low's cold front swept eastward from south-central Lower MI and northeastern IN to central Lake Erie and north-central OH. Ahead of the cold front and within the warm sector, isolated peak straight-line convective wind gusts of gale-force occurred along the Lake Erie shore from the Sandusky area to the Cleveland area. The gust in the Sandusky area was generated by a line of multicell thunderstorms that persisted generally eastward, while the gust in Cleveland was generated by a cluster of multicell rain showers that persisted northeastward, behind the aforementioned line of storms. These showers and storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate effective bulk shear and weak MUCAPE.
episodes.211080: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening hours of the 10th and early morning hours of the 11th, ahead of a dry line to the west and a cold front to the north, as an upper level disturbance moved into the area. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.
episodes.211081: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening hours of the 10th, and moved into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 11th. The thunderstorms developed ahead of a dry line to the west and a cold front to the north, as an upper level disturbance moved into the area. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.
episodes.211184: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
episodes.211220: An upper-level trough moved across northern Mexico and into West Texas, generating thunderstorms along and ahead of a dryline within a region of steep lapse rates and high instability. Isolated thunderstorms began forming east of the dryline around 1500CDT, including a long-tracked supercell which produced a brief tornado, strong winds, and a swath of large to very large hail from the Del Rio area to the Hill Country. A line of thunderstorms formed along the dryline over Val Verde County after 1900CDT which tracked across the southern Edwards Plateau and Hill Country through the evening, producing some strong winds before weakening near the I-35 corridor.
episodes.211264: A low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley region, pulling a cold front through the area. Showers and thunderstorms developed out in front of and along the front. Some storms produced instances of damaging wind gusts and heavy rainfall, leading to isolated flooding.
episodes.211526: An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
episodes.211588: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from quarter (1.00) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, a storm near Kewanee Illinois in Henry County produced a funnel cloud.
episodes.211592: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon on Tuesday producing hail that ranged in size from penny (0.88) to baseball (2.75) in diameter. There was a total of 10 reports with hail over 2.00 inches in diameter. During the early evening hours, one storm produced three different EF-1 tornadoes in Lee County near Donnellson.
episodes.211673: Warm sector convection ahead of an approaching cold front spawned thunderstorms, some of which were severe. An axis of up to 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE nosed up to Pittsburgh metro with strong effective shear as high as 60 knots. Hail and wind damage were reported with up to 1.5 inch hail, a measured 64 mph wind gust at a home weather station, and trees down on wires.
episodes.211674: Warm sector convection ahead of an approaching cold front spawned thunderstorms, some of which were severe. An axis of up to 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE nosed up to Pittsburgh metro with strong effective shear as high as 60 knots. Hail and wind damage were reported with up to 1.5 inch hail, a measured 64 mph wind gust at a home weather station, and trees down on wires.
episodes.211747: During the early evening hours on March 10th, a lone storm cell moved through portions of Grant County and produced quarter sized hail southwest of Platteville.
episodes.211800: A strong cold front moved into an early season warm, moist and unstable airmass. The result was a line of thunderstorms producing damaging wind gusts that moved through eastern Pennsylvania.
episodes.211822: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments. It's along those stronger segments where multiple marine locations were impacted by severe wind gusts.
episodes.211824: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 6 tornadoes were confirmed across southwest Mississippi and multiple  reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
episodes.211833: Numerous thunderstorms occurred over far southern WI as a warm front approached from the south. Repeated rounds of storms resulted in flash flooding in the Racine area, while some large hail occurred across far southern WI.
episodes.211865: A strong cold front swept through on March 11th, causing temperatures to plummet from the 60s into the 30s. A squall line (QLCS) developed ahead of the front, bringing damaging winds and embedded tornadoes to Wells and Jay counties in eastern Indiana.
episodes.211917: A seasonal strong cold front produced a line of thunderstorms. These storms produced isolated wind damage in portions of East Tennessee. As the front pushed into North Carolina, a sharp temperature drop yielded a changeover to snow at higher elevations in the Smokies, with a couple inches of snow accumulating.
episodes.211962: A series of upper level disturbances pushed through southeast Texas causing multiple days of stormy weather. A pair of severe weather reports were received. Behind the fast paced fronts that caused the unsettled weather, tides fell below normal.
episodes.211963: A series of upper disturbances and fast moving cold fronts cause multiple rounds of stormy weather across portions of Louisiana. Several severe storms occurred. Behind the fast paced systems, tides fell below normal.
episodes.212039: During the very early morning of March 11th, a QLCS pushed through northeastern Missouri and caused wind damage to several structures as it passed.
episodes.212041: During the early morning of March 11th, a QLCS pushed through portions of southern Illinois. The QLCS caused thunderstorm wind damage as it passed and produced 4 tornadoes.
episodes.212055: A cold front moved across the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours on March 11th. Ahead of the front, modest amounts of instability were present, with surface dewpoint temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s, allowing for between 500 and 1000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. With strong flow aloft, deep-layer shear was supportive of strong to severe storms, with shear values around 50-60 knots ahead of the front. Ultimately, ample cloudiness and stronger storms firing over the deep south limited the severe potential over much of Kentucky. However, a couple strong cells were able to make it into southeastern Kentucky, producing scattered instances of wind damage in the Lake Cumberland area.
episodes.212097: Multiple rounds of severe weather moved northeast across south-central and southeast Kansas during the evening hours March 10th. These severe thunderstorms produced numerous reports of large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.212105: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms extended from Southeast Oklahoma down across Central Texas late in the evening on March 10th, with the most organized threat area over Northeast Texas into Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. Effective storm-relative helicity ahead of the prominent line of thunderstorms was quite favorable for low-level rotation, and instability was rather strong as well. The VAD wind profile from the Shreveport Doppler Radar indicated a very favorable hodograph for rotating storms with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity over 250 m2/s2. As a result, severe thunderstorms produced an isolated tornado and some damaging wind gusts in parts of McCurtain County just prior to midnight on March 10th.
episodes.212108: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms extended from Southeast Oklahoma down across Central Texas late in the evening on March 10th and into the early morning on March 11th, with the most organized threat area over Northeast Texas into Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. Effective storm-relative helicity ahead of the prominent line of thunderstorms was quite favorable for low-level rotation, and instability was rather strong as well. The VAD wind profile from the Shreveport Doppler Radar indicated a very favorable hodograph for rotating storms with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity over 250 m2/s2. As a result, severe thunderstorms produced an isolated tornado and some damaging wind gusts in parts of Southwest Arkansas during the early morning hours on March 11th.
episodes.212109: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms extended from Southeast Oklahoma down across Central Texas late in the evening on March 10th and into the early morning on March 11th, with the most organized threat area over Northeast Texas into Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. Effective storm-relative helicity ahead of the prominent line of thunderstorms was quite favorable for low-level rotation, and instability was rather strong as well. As a result, severe thunderstorms produced some damaging wind gusts in parts of Deep East Texas during the early morning hours on March 11th.
episodes.212161: A surface low tracking eastward across the Midwest dragged a cold front south into Texas and east toward the Mid-South by the morning of March 11. Delayed arrival of the frontal boundary allowed diurnal instability to increase, interacting with 40 knots of bulk shear. As the front swept swiftly across the region, it triggered severe thunderstorms capable of producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across West Tennessee.
episodes.212244: Large hail and heavy rain impacted lower Michigan on March 10-11. Between 1 to 3 inches of rain fell in a short period of time, resulting in localized flash flooding and closed interstates with trapped cars in several counties.
episodes.212360: A dynamic storm system brought a sharp transition from record-breaking warmth to severe weather across eastern Kentucky on March 11th. Ahead of an approaching cold front, unseasonably warm air surged into the region on a potent low-level jet, with temperatures reaching record levels at London and Jackson. Widespread non-convective wind gusts between 30 and 50 mph occurred during the afternoon.||As the cold front moved in during the evening, a pre-frontal squall line (QLCS) developed in a high shear environment and tracked across the Commonwealth. The most intense measured wind gust was 70 mph at the London-Corbin Airport ASOS. Elsewhere, the storms resulted in structural damage, scattered downed trees, and a few power outages before a sharp cold front crossed the area, ushering in a much drier and colder airmass.
episodes.212428: Numerous thunderstorms occurred over far southern WI as a warm front approached from the south.

A destructive EF-3 tornado with estimated peak winds of 160 mph impacted portions of Newton and northwest Jasper Counties, most notably the community of Lake Village. After forming and causing EF-3 damage in Kankakee County, Illinois, this tornado crossed into Newton County between W 800 N Road and W 900 N Road near N 650 W Road. Upon entering the county, the tornado destroyed multiple outbuildings and significantly damaged multiple homes. On N 600 W Road, multiple homes were completely destroyed with debris blown clear of the foundations, consistent with EF-3 caliber winds. Nearby forested areas had almost all trees snapped or uprooted with some trees remaining standing with only stubs of a few large branches remaining, likely due to extensive lifted debris. Multiple homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was destroyed along N 500 W Road and along and near N 400 W Road. As the tornado crossed US-41 into the south side of Lake Village, it widened to approximately 1100 yards while damaging the roof and canopy of a gas station and a nearby retail building. Further north along N 300 W Road, multiple blocks of homes had significant roof damage and almost all trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado continued eastward into a wooded area near the Lugene Links Golf Course, where a continuous corridor of trees was entirely uprooted. As the tornado neared W 950 N Road and N 150 W Road, a few homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was completely destroyed. The tornado continued to produce damage to trees and outbuildings as it traveled northeastward through mainly rural portions of northern Newton County and northern portions of Roselawn. The tornado continued into Jasper County and dissipated shortly thereafter. It was on the ground for over 35 miles and, at its peak, spanned a half mile in diameter. The storm destroyed numerous homes and resulted in around a dozen injuries and three fatalities: one in Kankakee County and the other two near Lake Village.

A destructive EF-3 tornado was nearing the end of its lifecycle upon briefly moving into northwest Jasper County and dissipated shortly thereafter. After forming in Kankakee County and causing EF-3 caliber damage in Kankakee and Newton counties, this tornado crossed into far northwestern Jasper County between W 1100 N Road and W 1200 N Road. Along N 1200 W Road just east of I-65, a continuous corridor of trees was entirely uprooted, a few outbuildings were damaged, and the roof was removed from a house. In the community of Forest City, a continuous corridor of trees was uprooted, and a few residences had shingles removed. The tornado diminished in intensity as it moved northeast toward N 1100 W Road, and then dissipated just south of the intersection of N 1100 W Road and W 1300 N Road. The tornado resulted in three fatalities and around a dozen injuries, though none reported in Jasper County. The damage sustained in Jasper County was found to be on the order of EF-1 strength.

An EF-1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 110 mph tracked across northern Jasper County south of Stoutsburg, Wheatfield, and Dunns Bridge. This tornado began about 2 miles south of Stoutsburg along CR W 1000 N, where there was damage noted to a solar panel field and power poles. The tornado moved east-northeast, causing damage to a farmstead on CR N 200 W. The most significant damage from this tornado was noted just south of Wheatfield on the 0-100 block of CR W 1100 N and on the 1100 block of State Route 49, where numerous homes sustained considerable damage and numerous trees and power poles were downed. The tornado continued to damage solar panel fields, trees, power poles, and farmsteads as it moved toward the Starke County line, passing through the unincorporated community of Tefft. The tornado dissipated before reaching Starke County on the 500 block of CR E 1350 N. Three minor injuries were reported with the tornado.
The time of the event was estimated using radar.

A line of severe thunderstorms moved into McCurtain County, Oklahoma, late in the evening on March 10th. Circulations were embedded within this line of thunderstorms,  with one of which producing an EF2 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 118 mph that began on Old Golden Highway, resulting in snapped trees and the loss of shingles to a local residence. The tornado then continued east, reaching Thomas Road near the intersection of Old Golden Highway where more trees were snapped and uprooted and a barn/shed experienced damage to the roof. The tornado then began to pick up in intensity as it moved across Oak Hill Road where numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. As the tornado then continued northeast towards Rhoden Road, it caused significant damage to a family residence, resulting in the collapse of most exterior walls and an injury to the occupant who had to be airlifted to the hospital. Trees were then uprooted and fell onto this residence, causing additional damage. Next door to this home, significant damage was found to other structures as well as additional tree damage. Just before reaching Rhoden Road, another residence was damaged, where areas of the roof were uplifted, multiple trees were snapped and uprooted, and the neighboring barn experienced significant roof damage. The tornado then moved north/northeast of the road, pushing a small outbuilding off of its foundation and snapping and uprooting more trees before lifting as it crossed Highway 3.

A supercell thunderstorm moved through northern Montgomery and northwestern Howard Counties in Maryland during the evening hours of Wednesday March 11, 2026. The bow echo and associated downbursts/thunderstorm wind gusts caused sporadic tree damage from 60-80mph gusts, and created a brief EF-1 tornado, with focused tornadic damage near Cooksville in northwestern Howard County. On March 12, staff from the National Weather Service Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast Office conducted a ground survey of the storm damage. The survey started near Damascus and extended through northwestern Howard County. There were numerous instances of trees uprooted or snapped, as well as damage resulting from downed trees. Tree fall was generally in the direction of the storm's easterly movement. Ground evidence suggested the thunderstorm produced scattered wind damage along its path from 60 to 80 mph wind gusts. However, as the storm continued east-northeastward, crossing the interchange of I-70 and MD-97, damage was observed 300 yards southwest of Old Frederick Road, crossing Old Frederick Road between Forsythe Road and Underwood Road. Here, along a treeline to the southwest of Old Frederick Road, approximately 50 trees were uprooted or snapped across an approximately 100 yard wide swath. Several of the uprooted trees fell at right angles to each other. Additional trees were snapped or uprooted near residences to the northeast of the road. The tornado appeared to have briefly lifted before touching down a final time at a residence on Underwood Road, where several trees were uprooted and snapped in multiple directions. This damage is indicative of a low-end EF-1 tornado. Additional to the ground survey, Doppler radar information from KLWX (Sterling VA radar) and TBWI (FAA BWI radar) was analyzed. Radar showed a powerful storm with broad rotation aloft along its path. From radar analysis coupled with ground observations, it was determined that an EF-1 tornado formed at 7:06pm and lifted at 7:08pm, with estimated winds up to 90 mph, a path length of 0.4 miles, and a maximum width of 100 yards. Special thanks to Howard County Office of Emergency Management for their assistance. Additionally, thanks to the trained spotters, media, and public that sent in reports of damage.

A supercell thunderstorm moved through northern Montgomery, northwestern Howard, and southeast Carroll Counties in Maryland during the evening hours of Wednesday March 11, 2026. The bow echo and associated downbursts/thunderstorm wind gusts caused sporadic tree damage from 60 to 80 mph gusts, and created both a brief EF-1 tornado near Cooksville in northwestern Howard County for which there is a previous report, and this EF-0 tornado in Prospect Hills MD, in southeastern Carroll County in the Patapsco Valley State Park. As the storm crossed into southeastern Carroll County, it produced a brief tornado in Patapsco Valley State Park, with an EF-0 touching down at 7:14 pm. In the park, just east of Marriottsville Rd, there were numerous trees uprooted and snapped. The most intense area of tree damage was right along the entrance drive in the McKeldin Area. Peak winds in this area were estimated to be 80 mph. Several trees were snapped down in multiple directions in a path up to 75 yards wide. Shortly after, the tornado lifted at 7:15 pm and no further tornadic damage was noted. However, sporadic wind damage in the direction of storm motion continued to occur with the winds from the severe thunderstorm. Special thanks to Montgomery and Carroll County Offices of Emergency Management for their assistance and damage assessments.

The damage path of an EF-0 tornado with estimated peak winds near 85 mph and max width was identified on high resolution satellite imagery in northeast Wilkinson County, just south of Perrytown, MS. Evident damage and displacement to trees were identified near Turkey Creek Rd which extended to the east-southeast through to Tom Crum Rd which was closely collocated to a strong area of rotation on KHDC. The majority of this damage path was inaccessible to ground survey and thus is rated via identifiable damage via satellite.

This tornado began east of US Highway 167, southwest of Fordyce. The tornado tracked northeast across several county roads as well as state Highway 274, Highway 205, Highway 8, Highway 97, and Highway 189. As the tornado moved across these areas it did extensive damage to pine trees as well as some hardwood trees. A few outbuildings were damaged and some minor roof damage was noted on a few residences. As the tornado moved across Highway 97 a few trees were knocked down onto the roadway. A two vehicle accident occurred due to this, with no reported injuries. The tornado ended around the Saline River. This tornado was rated EF1 with max wind gusts estimated of 105 mph.
